```{r setup, include=FALSE, error=FALSE}
options(warn = 0)
all_times <- list()  # store elapsed seconds for each chunk
knitr::knit_hooks$set(time_it = local({
  start <- NULL
  function(before, options) {
    if (!isTRUE(options$time_it) || identical(options$eval, FALSE)) return(NULL)
    if (before) {
      start <<- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
      return(NULL)
    }
    seconds <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - start
    all_times[[options$label]] <<- seconds
    sprintf("\n\n<p class=\"chunk-timing\"><small><sup>Elapsed: %.2f s</sup></small></p>\n\n", seconds)
  }
}))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  time_it = TRUE,
  tidy = FALSE,
  fig.width = 10,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  error = FALSE
)
```

# Introduction

This vignette walks you through our Single-cell Sample-Level Inference using Density Estimation (scSLIDE) workflow, a computational method that performs sample-level analysis for single-cell data. Given a multi-sample single-cell dataset, scSLIDE first constructs a cell-type-oriented embedding (via reference mapping, integration, or unsupervised dimension reduction) and a disease-oriented embedding (via a supervised learning method, partial least squares, PLS). It then combines these two embeddings into a joint WNN embedding, placing cells in a joint space where their distances reflect both cell-type and disease-state similarity. Next, we use a randomly sketched subset of cells (called 'landmarks', originally proposed by [Yi & Stanley](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10680595/)) and quantify the cell density near each landmark for each sample. This produces a landmark-by-donor density matrix that quantitatively captures the similarity and differences among samples. Sample-level analyses such as clustering, pseudo-trajectory inference, and differential expression testing can then be performed on this sample-level embedding. You can read more about our method in [this preprint](https://doi.org/10.64898/2025.12.10.693462).

# Setup and Library Loading

First, we need to install the version of Seurat that contains the scSLIDE module, load all necessary libraries, and set up the working environment.

```{r install-scslide, eval=FALSE}
# make sure you install Seurat from the following branch:
remotes::install_github(repo = "satijalab/seurat-rewrite@merge_scSLIDE", 
                       force = TRUE,
                       INSTALL_opts = "--preclean")

# some other packages that will be used in this vignette can be installed using the following commands:
# devtools::install_github("satijalab/AzimuthAPI")
# BiocManager::install("destiny")
# install.packages(c("princurve", "ggridges"))

```

```{r packages}
library(Seurat) # make sure this is the scSLIDE-compatible version
library(AzimuthAPI)
library(BPCells)
library(princurve)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggridges)

```

# Data Loading and Initial Processing

For demonstration, we will use a subset (~104k cells) of a COVID-19 dataset generated by [Ahern et al 2022 Cell](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35216673/) as an example for our workflow. This subset can be downloaded from [this link](https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/9tnda21yoy48s0zepvjs4/Raw_count_Subset_104k_Ahern_2022_Cell.rds?rlkey=vfwvjdhyitd4qi8g9clko0hil&st=4b03u92v&dl=0). The dataset consists of 40 donors: 10 healthy controls ('HV') and 10 patients from each of 3 different COVID severity groups ("MILD", "SEV", "CRIT").

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE}
object <- readRDS("Raw_count_Subset_104k_Ahern_2022_Cell.rds")
```

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE}
object <- NormalizeData(object) 
```

# Cell Type Annotation with Azimuth

We will use the [pan-human Azimuth cloud tool](https://satijalab.org/pan_human_azimuth/) to annotate our data and obtain a cell-type-oriented embedding. You can read more about this reference-mapping method in [this paper](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.07.16.738997v1.full). Note that you are welcome to use simple PCA or any other integration/reference-mapping method to obtain such an embedding.

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE}
object <- CloudAzimuth(object)

# Get the top 2000 highly variable genes 
object <- FindVariableFeatures(object, nfeatures = 2000)
```


# Prepare the Single-Cell Data for Sample-Level Analysis

We provide a wrapper function called `PrepareSampleObject()` that performs all the cell-level pre-processing steps required for sample-level embedding generation. In brief, the wrapper (optionally) identifies additional highly variable genes associated with the phenotype of interest through correlation testing, (optionally) creates a training subset for PLS (to balance the number of cells from each sample), selects a landmark cell subset via [geometric sketching](https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/seurat5_sketch_analysis), performs PLS to capture response-relevant variation, and constructs a [weighted multi-modal nearest neighbor](https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/weighted_nearest_neighbor_analysis) graph between the landmark cells and the full dataset. The function returns a Seurat object containing the landmark assay and a cell-to-landmark WNN graph, both needed for the subsequent sample-level object generation.

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE}
object <- PrepareSampleObject(object = object, 
                             assay = "RNA", 
                             add.hvg = T, 
                             group.by.CorTest = "azimuth_label", 
                             Y = "Disease", 
                             sketch.training = T, 
                             group.by.Sketch = "Donor", 
                             ncells.per.group = 1000, 
                             ncells.landmark = 2000, 
                             ncomp = 20, 
                             pls.function = "cppls", 
                             k.nn = 5, 
                             name.reduction.1 = "azimuth_embed", 
                             dims.reduction.1 = 1:128,
                             fix.wnn.weights = c(0.5, 0.5), 
                             verbose = T)
```

<details><summary style="font-size: 18px;"><strong>What does <code>PrepareSampleObject()</code> actually do?</strong></summary>

The `PrepareSampleObject()` function is a high-level wrapper that streamlines the cell-level data preparation process through four key steps:

1. **Training subset creation:** Performs uniform sketching to obtain a representative training subset for efficient PLS learning (optional)
2. **Landmark cell selection:** Uses leverage-score sketching to identify a diverse subset of landmark cells that capture the dataset's heterogeneity
3. **Response-oriented embedding:** Conducts PLS learning to generate embeddings that capture variation relevant to the specified response variable
4. **Neighbor graph construction:** Builds a weighted multi-modal nearest neighbor graph connecting landmark cells to all other cells in the dataset

The resulting neighbor graph serves as the foundation for generating sample-level landmark matrices in downstream analysis.

For users who need fine-grained control over individual parameters, the following step-by-step workflow demonstrates how to manually execute each component of `PrepareSampleObject()` with custom settings.

<h3>Data Sketching Procedures</h3>

Next, we sketch the data using two different procedures. The first procedure draws a random subset of cells from each donor (e.g., n = 1000), ensuring that the number of cells is approximately balanced across donors for supervised learning. This step is optional if the cell numbers are already balanced, but we recommend it for efficiency.

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
object = SketchDataByGroup(object, assay = "RNA", ncells = 1000, sketched.assay = "TRAINING",
                           method = "Uniform", group.by = "Donor", verbose = FALSE)
```

The second procedure performs leverage-score-based sketching to select a representative subset of cells (called landmark cells) that covers the diverse cell states in the data. Later, we will generate sample-level embeddings using these landmarks.

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
object = SketchData(object, assay = "TRAINING", ncells = 2000, sketched.assay = "LANDMARK",
                    method = "LeverageScore", verbose = FALSE)
```

<h3>Disease-Relevant Gene Selection</h3>

We can obtain additional disease-relevant genes to enhance PLS learning (in case the HVGs are not all relevant to the phenotype). If the variable features are already sufficiently informative, you can omit this step.

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
deg_list = QuickCorTest(object, assay = "TRAINING", layer = "data", group.by = "azimuth_label", Y = "Disease", cor.cutoff = 0.2, verbose = FALSE)
all_HVG = union(VariableFeatures(object), deg_list)
```

<h3>Supervised Learning with Partial Least Squares (PLS)</h3>

We apply supervised PLS learning to the TRAINING data to obtain disease-oriented low-dimensional embeddings. `RunPLS()` supports three different PLS algorithms: standard PLS ('plsr'), canonical PLS ('cppls'), and sparse PLS ('spls'). Please see the `RunPLS()` manual for details.

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
DefaultAssay(object) = "TRAINING"
object = ScaleData(object, features = all_HVG)
object = RunPLS(object = object, assay = "TRAINING", features = all_HVG, 
                ncomp = 20, 
                Y = c("Disease"), 
                pls.function = "cppls",
                verbose = FALSE)
```

<h3>Projection to Full Dataset</h3>

Now we project the learned PLS onto the full dataset and append the projected PLS embeddings.

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
proj.pls <- ProjectCellEmbeddings(
  query = object,
  query.assay = "RNA",
  reference = object,
  reference.assay = "TRAINING",
  reduction = "pls",
  dims = 1:20,
  scale = T,
  normalization.method = "LogNormalize",
  verbose = T
)

# Append the projected PLS embeddings to the full data
object[['proj.pls']] <- CreateDimReducObject(embeddings = proj.pls, key = "pPLS_", assay = "RNA")
rm(proj.pls)
gc()
```

<h3>Joint Embedding Construction with Weighted Nearest Neighbors</h3>

Having obtained the cell-type-oriented and disease-oriented embeddings, we now generate a joint embedding that accounts for both types of information, placing cells in a joint space where their distances reflect their overall similarity. We use the weighted nearest neighbor (WNN) procedure originally developed by Hao & Hao et al, Cell 2021. Instead of running the original WNN procedure, here we modify it so that the 'modality weights' of the two embeddings are both fixed at 0.5, ensuring they contribute equally to the WNN embedding (you can set other values or let the algorithm learn the weights dynamically). The function then returns a WNN graph between the landmark cells and all other cells in the dataset. 

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
DefaultAssay(object) = "RNA"

object = FindmmNN(object,
                  sketch.assay = "LANDMARK",
                  reduction.list = list("azimuth_embed", "proj.pls"),
                  k.nn = 5,
                  nn.name = "weighted.nn",
                  dims.list = list(1:128, 1:20),
                  fix.wnn.weights = c(0.5, 0.5))
```

<h3>What if we only want to use a single modality to generate the NN graph?</h3>
By default, scSLIDE uses the WNN embedding to generate the sample-level embedding. However, if you prefer to use a single modality instead (e.g., only the PLS embedding, or any custom embedding from another method), you can do so by switching from `FindmmNN()` to `FindsmNN()` and passing in a single embedding. This returns a standard kNN graph based on that embedding, which can be used directly for downstream sample-level embedding generation.

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
DefaultAssay(object) = "RNA"

object = FindsmNN(object,
                  sketch.assay = "LANDMARK",
                  reduction= "proj.pls",
                  k.nn = 5,
                  dims = 1:20, 
                  nn.name = "single.nn")
```

# Sample-Level Embedding Generation

Once a WNN graph is constructed, we can generate a sample-level density matrix. Given the asymmetric landmark-by-cell WNN graph, scSLIDE aggregates over cells to obtain a landmark-by-sample density matrix (i.e., m landmarks by n samples) by binarizing adjacency (neighbor = 1, else 0) and summing per sample. Each entry in this landmark-by-sample matrix measures the cell density near each landmark for a given donor.

The function `GenerateSampleObject()` builds this sample-level object from the WNN graph specified by `nn.name =`. It can also look up donor-level metadata in the original single-cell object and append it to the sample-level object (optional), and it can apply a Chi-squared normalization (based on the Poisson distribution of a contingency table) to the count matrix (optional; standard log-normalization is also supported).

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE}
sample_obj = GenerateSampleObject(object = object, 
                                  sketch.assay = "LANDMARK", 
                                  nn.name = "weighted.nn", 
                                  group.by = "Donor", 
                                  rename.group.by = "azimuth_label", 
                                  k.nn = 5, 
                                  normalization.method = "ChiSquared",
                                  add.meta.data = TRUE,
                                  return.seurat = T)
# Center the data
sample_obj = ScaleData(sample_obj, features = rownames(sample_obj), do.scale = F, do.center = T)
```


# Diffusion Map Analysis

To better infer a trajectory for the sample-level data, instead of standard PCA we perform Diffusion Map (a non-linear, unsupervised dimensional reduction method originally proposed by [Haghverdi et al, Bioinformatics](https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/31/18/2989/241305) to capture single-cell trajectories).

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE}
sample_obj = RunDiffusionMap(sample_obj, assay = "LMC", layer = "scale.data", features = rownames(sample_obj), ncomp = 10)
```

By visualizing the Diffusion Map components, we can see that DC1 captures case-control status, DC2 captures some COVID heterogeneity (not related to severity), and DC3 captures COVID severity.

```{r fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
DimPlot(sample_obj, reduction = "DiffMap", group.by = "Disease") +
  DimPlot(sample_obj, reduction = "DiffMap", group.by = "Disease", dims = c(1, 3))
```

We append DC1-3 to the metadata and analyze their relationships with clinical variables.

```{r}
# Append DC1-3 to the metadata
sample_obj[['traj_DC1']] = sample_obj@reductions$DiffMap@cell.embeddings[, 1]
sample_obj[['traj_DC2']] = sample_obj@reductions$DiffMap@cell.embeddings[, 2]
sample_obj[['traj_DC3']] = sample_obj@reductions$DiffMap@cell.embeddings[, 3]
```

The following plots show that DC2 is related to TimeSinceOnset and DC3 is related to severity:

```{r fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
# Showing DC2 is related to TimeSinceOnset and DC3 is related to severity
p1 = FeatureScatter(sample_obj, 
               feature1 = "traj_DC2", 
               feature2 = "TimeSinceOnset", 
               group.by = "Disease", 
               cells = colnames(sample_obj)[sample_obj$Disease != "HV"], 
               pt.size = 2)

p2 = ggplot(sample_obj@meta.data[sample_obj$Disease != "HV", ]) +
  geom_density_ridges(aes(x = traj_DC3, y = Disease, fill = Disease), scale = 0.9) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 15), 
        text = element_text(size = 13), 
        axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 1, vjust = 1, angle = 45),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 13)) 
print(p1 + p2)
```

<details><summary>Fitting a joint pseudo-trajectory using principal curve</summary>

<h3>Principal Curve Fitting</h3>

If you want to explore whether multiple DCs can be merged, you can fit a principal curve to the top few DCs to obtain a single joint pseudo-trajectory. Here we fit such a curve to the top 2 DCs and append it to the object.

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
princurve_res = princurve::principal_curve(sample_obj[['DiffMap']]@cell.embeddings[, 1:2],
                                           plot = F, maxit = 20, trace = T)
sample_obj[['traj_overall']] = princurve_res$lambda
DimPlot(sample_obj, reduction = "DiffMap", group.by = "Disease")  +
  geom_path(aes(x = princurve_res$s[princurve_res$ord, 1], y = princurve_res$s[princurve_res$ord, 2]))
```

</details>


# Differential Expression Analysis Setup

Finally, we can perform differential expression (DE) analysis to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) that change along the pseudo-trajectory we inferred. We do this for each DC separately, since we believe they represent three distinct biological variations.

First, we obtain the pseudobulked expression data from the original single-cell data:

```{r}
bulk_obj = AggregateExpression(object, assays = "RNA", group.by = c("Donor", "azimuth_label"), return.seurat = T)
```

```{r}
# Append the metadata to pseudobulked object 
mdata = object@meta.data[, c("Donor", "azimuth_label")]
mdata = mdata[!duplicated(mdata), ]
rownames(mdata) = paste0(gsub(pattern = "_", replacement = "-", mdata$Donor),
                         "_",
                         gsub(pattern = "_", replacement = "-", mdata$azimuth_label))
bulk_obj = AddMetaData(bulk_obj, metadata  = mdata)

bulk_obj$nCount_RNA = colSums(x = bulk_obj, slot = "counts")  # nCount_RNA
bulk_obj$nFeature_RNA = colSums(x = LayerData(object = bulk_obj, layer = "counts") > 0)  # nFeature_RNA
```

## DE Analysis for CD14 Monocytes

Then we run the DE analysis one cell type at a time, using "CD14 monocytes" as an example.

```{r}
sub_bulk_obj = subset(bulk_obj, subset = azimuth_label == "CD14 monocyte")

# Add metadata from sample-level object to pseudobulk object
new_mdata = merge(sub_bulk_obj@meta.data[, c("Donor"), drop = F],
                  sample_obj@meta.data[, c("Donor", "Age", "Sex", "Disease", "traj_DC1", "traj_DC2", "traj_DC3")],
                  by = "Donor",
                  all.x = T,
                  sort = FALSE)
sub_bulk_obj = AddMetaData(sub_bulk_obj, metadata = new_mdata)
sub_bulk_obj$log_count = log10(sub_bulk_obj$nCount_RNA)
```

We can now run trajectory DE tests for DC1, DC2, and DC3. Note that we remove healthy donors for DC2 and DC3 to concentrate on within-COVID heterogeneity.

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE}
# Run trajectory DE test for DC1
de_results = TrajDETest(sub_bulk_obj, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts",
                        traj.var = "traj_DC1", latent.vars = c("Age", "Sex", "log_count"))

# Run trajectory DE tests for DC2 and DC3
non_health_idx = Cells(sub_bulk_obj)[sub_bulk_obj$Disease != "HV"]
de_results2 = TrajDETest(sub_bulk_obj, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts",
                         traj.var = "traj_DC2", latent.vars = c("Age", "Sex", "log_count"),
                         samples = non_health_idx)

de_results3 = TrajDETest(sub_bulk_obj, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts",
                         traj.var = "traj_DC3", latent.vars = c("Age", "Sex", "log_count"),
                         samples = non_health_idx)
```

From the DE results, we identify the top up- and down-regulated DEGs for visualization:

```{r}
# Identify the top up- and down-regulated DEGs for visualization
de_results$sign = sign(de_results$beta_Traj)
de_results = de_results[order(de_results$sign, de_results$p_Traj), ]
DEG_DC1 = c(de_results$gene_ID[de_results$sign > 0][1:20], 
            de_results$gene_ID[de_results$sign < 0][20:1])

de_results2$sign = sign(de_results2$beta_Traj)
de_results2 = de_results2[order(de_results2$sign, de_results2$p_Traj), ]
DEG_DC2 = c(de_results2$gene_ID[de_results2$sign > 0][1:20], 
            de_results2$gene_ID[de_results2$sign < 0][20:1])

de_results3$sign = sign(de_results3$beta_Traj)
de_results3 = de_results3[order(de_results3$sign, de_results3$p_Traj), ]
DEG_DC3 = c(de_results3$gene_ID[de_results3$sign > 0][1:20], 
            de_results3$gene_ID[de_results3$sign < 0][20:1])
```

We provide a wrapper visualization function, `PlotAnnotatedHeatmap()` (which adopts the style and color scheme of [Scillus](https://github.com/xmc811/Scillus), a package that is no longer maintained for Seurat > v5.3), to generate a pseudobulk heatmap for DC1 (donors are ordered by DC1):

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# Heatmap visualization for DC1 (donors are ordered based on DC1)
sub_bulk_obj = ScaleData(sub_bulk_obj, features = DEG_DC1)

library(ComplexHeatmap)
library(circlize)

PlotAnnotatedHeatmap(
    object      = sub_bulk_obj,
    features    = DEG_DC1, 
    sort.by     = "traj_DC1",
    anno.var    = "Disease", 
    anno.colors = list(c("#f8766d", "cornsilk", "#7cae02", "blue1", "#01bfc4", "#c77cff")), 
    hm.colors   = c("blue", "white", "red")
)

```

Heatmap visualization for DC2 and DC3 (healthy donors are removed):

```{r message = FALSE, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
# Heatmap visualization for DC2 and DC3 (healthy donors are removed)
sub_bulk_obj2 = subset(sub_bulk_obj, cells = non_health_idx)
sub_bulk_obj2 = ScaleData(sub_bulk_obj2, features = c(DEG_DC1, DEG_DC2, DEG_DC3))

PlotAnnotatedHeatmap(
    object      = sub_bulk_obj2,
    features    = DEG_DC2, 
    sort.by     = "traj_DC2",
    anno.var    = "Disease", 
    anno.colors = list(c("cornsilk", "#7cae02", "blue1", "#01bfc4", "#c77cff")), 
    hm.colors   = c("blue", "white", "red")
)

PlotAnnotatedHeatmap(
    object      = sub_bulk_obj2,
    features    = DEG_DC3, 
    sort.by     = "traj_DC3",
    anno.var    = "Disease", 
    anno.colors = list(c("cornsilk", "#7cae02", "blue1", "#01bfc4", "#c77cff")),
    hm.colors   = c("blue", "white", "red")
)

```
